title: The consumer-voter is killing German politics
gist: Chancellor Merz's collapse in popularity (about 10% satisfaction) mirrors Starmer's and South Korea's Lee Jae-myung's, which the author attributes to a structural shift of voters from citizens to consumers of politics amplified by social media, favouring permanent-campaign politicians like Hungary's Péter Magyar.

insights.claim: After a series of heavy state-election defeats, only 10% of Germans are satisfied with Chancellor Merz; in a Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania post-election survey just 1% thought he helped the CDU while 80% saw him as a liability, and a premature exit after about 1.5 years is a serious possibility.
insights.speaker: Lukas Schmelter
insights.so_what: German government stability and the reform and fiscal agenda are at risk; watch coalition and leadership change.
insights.locator: Only ten per cent of Germans are still satisfied with Merz

insights.claim: Merz and Starmer rose and fell similarly: both reached office circuitously, ran against failed governments, promised rapid change, had no coherent governing plan, and suffered communication blunders and poor personnel choices, with approval falling at an unprecedented pace.
insights.speaker: Lukas Schmelter
insights.so_what: Centrist 'stability' mandates decay fast; expect short political half-lives for governing-centre leaders.
insights.locator: Just as there are parallels to be found in their respective rises

insights.claim: South Korea's President Lee Jae-myung, in office since June of last year, saw approval fall from 67% to 37% within four months, which the author uses to argue the pattern spans parliamentary, Westminster and presidential systems and is therefore structural.
insights.speaker: Lukas Schmelter
insights.so_what: Cross-country evidence that government honeymoon periods are collapsing.
insights.locator: Merz and Starmer are by no means isolated cases

insights.claim: Post-Cold War complacency turned western publics from active citizens into consumers of politics who treat it like a streaming subscription or delivery app and expect immediate results, which makes any government's popularity structurally hard to sustain.
insights.speaker: Lukas Schmelter
insights.so_what: Reform-heavy agendas (fiscal, defence) face voters who punish slow delivery; discount durable political capital.
insights.quote: they expect results, and they expect them immediately, on demand
insights.locator: Many in western publics no longer see themselves as citizens

insights.claim: Short, emotional media and social media erode the reasoning public sphere (Habermas's shift from reasoning to consuming public), producing Canetti-style online mobs and a 'double mob' of mutually dependent culture-war camps that algorithms reward, leaving centrist governing figures as targets of both.
insights.speaker: Lukas Schmelter
insights.so_what: Algorithmic polarisation penalises centrist governance and boosts populist and extreme politics.
insights.locator: What has taken its place is the mob behaviour

insights.claim: Politicians who treat voters as consumers and never stop campaigning thrive; Hungary's Péter Magyar, five months after beating Orbán, retains his popularity by streaming constantly and turning government business into clickbait, a 'Netflix democracy'.
insights.speaker: Lukas Schmelter
insights.so_what: Hungary's new government is currently resilient, but the author expects such popularity to peak eventually.
insights.locator: Hungary provides a case study for this phenomenon

insights.claim: Canetti's work implies the permanent-broadcast model has a natural end point, since a mass holds together only while growing and directed and even popular shows peak and decline.
insights.speaker: Lukas Schmelter
insights.so_what: Expect even social-media-native leaders' approval to erode eventually; do not extrapolate current popularity.
insights.locator: Whether this spells the salvation of representative democracy

themes.theme: Post-Cold War decline in elite quality

insights.claim: The peace dividend lowered the stakes of politics and filled it with mediocre technocrats unsuited to today's geopolitical and technological shifts, while the same era left the voting public less suited to upholding liberal democracy, especially in Europe.
insights.speaker: Lukas Schmelter
insights.so_what: Both supply and demand sides of politics are degraded, raising the odds of volatile electoral outcomes.
